## silk-road
### Trade across the ancient world

Move through four periods to explore how goods connected distant societies, from the Bronze Age Mediterranean to the medieval Silk Roads.

> Selected exchanges around each date. Routes are schematic, not borders; dots show direction, not trade volume or speed.

[Sources and trade notes ↗](./silk-road-sources.md)

## silk-road-bronze-age
### The world that made bronze

Bronze joined **copper and tin** from distant sources. Cypriot copper, imported tin, Egyptian gold, glass, timber and crafted goods connected the Aegean, Egypt and western Asia.

Around **1200 BCE**, warfare, drought, shortages and political upheaval disrupted this interconnected world. Trade breakdown was part of the crisis; its causes and local outcomes remain debated.

- **Tin** · Britain & Central Asia → Mediterranean
- **Copper** · Cyprus → neighbouring markets
- **Gold** · Nubia & Egypt → Levant
- **Glass** · Egypt → Mediterranean
- **Timber** · Levant → Egypt
- **Textiles & pottery** · Mesopotamia & Aegean → ports

> Fainter tin lines show proposed supply chains. British tin has new scientific support; the eastern corridor from Central Asia and Afghanistan through Iran and Mesopotamia remains a debated reconstruction. Exact sources, itineraries and volumes are uncertain. Dot frequency is illustrative.

[Sources and trade notes ↗](./silk-road-sources.md)

## silk-road-antiquity
### Rome, India and Han China

Silk passed west through Central Asian intermediaries; Roman gold, silver and manufactured goods travelled east. The **Parthian and Kushan worlds** linked these exchanges with India and Han China.

Roads and rivers fed regional markets. Ships joined Roman Egypt to Indian ports through the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. **Ctesiphon**, rather than the later city of Baghdad, anchors Mesopotamia here.

- **Silk** · China → west and south
- **Gold & silver** · Roman world → east
- **Glass, copper & tin** · Mediterranean → India
- **Horses** · Fergana → China
- **Spices & cotton** · India → Roman world

> Selected corridors around 150 CE, not imperial borders or single journeys. Random dots show direction; their frequency does not represent volume. Constantinople and the Sui–Tang canal network belong to later periods.

[Sources and trade notes ↗](./silk-road-sources.md)

## silk-road-early-middle-ages
### Rivers, caravans and sea lanes

**Baghdad, Constantinople and late Tang China** belong to a different trading world. The Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean link western Asia with India and southern China; silk is also produced in the Byzantine world.

Northern rivers connect Baltic traders and Rus’ communities with **Volga Bulgar, Khazar and Central Asian markets**. Furs and enslaved people travelled south; silver moved north. The map’s northern colour follows furs only.

- **Silk** · China & Byzantium → wider markets
- **Gold & silver** · western & Central Asia → north and India
- **Horses** · Central Asia → China
- **Spices & cotton** · India → western Asia and China
- **Furs** · northern forests → southern markets

> Representative networks of the 9th–10th centuries, centred on 900 CE. River routes include portages. Connections crossed political frontiers; random dot frequency does not measure trade volume.

[Sources and trade notes ↗](./silk-road-sources.md)

## silk-road-high-middle-ages
### Across the Mongol world

The **Golden Horde and other Mongol states** connected markets across the steppes. The lower Volga, Black Sea ports and Central Asia formed major links, with merchants continuing toward Venice, Genoa and Constantinople.

Yuan China’s cities and the port of **Quanzhou** joined an expanding maritime network. Silk, ceramics and Indian goods circulated through Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean and western Asia.

- **Silk** · China → overland and maritime markets
- **Gold & silver** · Mediterranean & Gulf → trading partners
- **Horses** · Central Asia → China
- **Spices & cotton** · India → western Asia and China
- **Furs** · northern forests → Volga & Central Asia
- **Ceramics** · China → Indian Ocean ports

> Selected networks of the 13th–14th centuries, centred on 1300 CE. Wars and changing borders interrupted trade; these exchanges do not imply one continuously open or unified empire. Random dot frequency is illustrative.

[Sources and trade notes ↗](./silk-road-sources.md)

## french-polynesia
### A world across the Pacific

Polynesian voyagers connected islands across an immense ocean. From Hawaiʻi to Aotearoa New Zealand and Rapa Nui, related cultures grew through exploration, settlement and exchange. Tahiti sits within this wider island world.

> The Polynesian Triangle: a broad cultural region, not a single empire or an exact boundary.

[Explore the Polynesian Triangle ↗](https://teara.govt.nz/en/map/43839/polynesian-languages)

## origin-of-mankind
### Out of Africa, across the world

Human history includes repeated dispersals out of Africa. Earlier relatives, including **Homo erectus**, reached Eurasia long before our species.

The lines here show only **Homo sapiens**: successive migrations across Eurasia, into Sahul and later the Americas. Some broad corridors overlapped with earlier dispersals, but the routes and destinations were not identical.

Our species emerged among connected African populations. This East African dot anchors the story, rather than marking a single birthplace for all humans.

- **Early dispersals** · before 70,000 years ago
- **Eurasia & Sahul** · broadly 70,000–40,000 years ago
- **Further migrations** · later Ice Age & Holocene

> Schematic corridors on modern coastlines. Dates overlap; moving dots show direction, not speed or a shared timeline. Some routes remain debated.

[Sources and route notes ↗](./human-migrations-sources.md)

## ancient-egypt
### Egypt at its greatest reach

Under **Thutmose III**, in the 15th century BCE, Egyptian power stretched from Nubia’s Fourth Cataract to the Euphrates. The Nile connected the kingdom’s heartland with its southern territories, while campaigns secured influence across the Levant.

> Approximate maximum reach, including dependent rulers. Control varied across the shaded region.

[Sources and boundary notes ↗](./territory-tours-sources.md)

## mesopotamia
### The Neo-Assyrian Empire

In the **7th century BCE**, Assyrian kings ruled a vast empire from Mesopotamia. At its height, their reach extended through the Levant and into Egypt, linking many peoples through conquest, administration and tribute.

> Approximate maximum reach under Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal. Egypt was held briefly; some territories were governed through local rulers.

[Sources and boundary notes ↗](./territory-tours-sources.md)

## iceland-to-vinland
### Westward to Vinland

Norse voyagers crossed the North Atlantic through the **Shetlands, Faroes, Iceland and Greenland**. Around a thousand years ago, journeys continued past Baffin Island and Labrador to shores already inhabited for millennia, reaching northern Newfoundland.

> Schematic sea corridors across several generations. L’Anse aux Meadows is an archaeological anchor; the full extent of Vinland remains uncertain.

[Sources and voyage notes ↗](./territory-tours-sources.md)

## amazon-mouth
### A continent flowing into one river

From the Andes to the Atlantic, tributaries gather water across the **Amazon drainage basin**. The shaded area follows the watershed: land whose rivers feed the Amazon, crossing today’s national borders.

> Simplified HydroBASINS boundary, about 5.9 million km². This is the drainage basin, not the extent of the rainforest; the Tocantins basin is separate.

[Data and boundary notes ↗](./territory-tours-sources.md)

## india
### Ashoka’s Mauryan Empire

Around **250 BCE**, the Mauryan Empire linked much of the Indian subcontinent, from the northwest to Bengal and deep into the Deccan. After the devastating conquest of Kalinga, Ashoka’s inscriptions proclaimed a new emphasis on moral government and restraint.

> Approximate extent under Ashoka. The far south and Sri Lanka remained outside; authority within the empire was uneven.

[Sources and boundary notes ↗](./territory-tours-sources.md)

## china
### The Qing at their greatest extent

During **Qianlong’s reign**, the Qing expanded into a vast, multiethnic empire. By the late 18th century, its territories included China’s heartland, Manchuria, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang.

> Approximate historical extent, with varied forms of rule. Tributary neighbors are excluded; this is not a map of modern borders.

[Sources and boundary notes ↗](./territory-tours-sources.md)
